column6: These different representations of DSEs are possible because of the way TEI-Publisher works. Indeed, one of key-concepts of this software

column7: is the one of web-components Web-components are a W3C standard. They can be seen
as blocks that contain the HTML code, the CSS and the Javascript needed by a specific
functionality to function.. They can be considered as blocks, each one
corresponding to a functionality. For example, there is a web-component for displaying
facsimiles, another for creating a map, and another for adding a simple search
bar A list of the TEI-Publisher’s web-components can be
found through an API: https://unpkg.com/@teipublisher/pb-components@1.30.3/dist/api.html [Accessed 28
march 2023].. These blocks can be combined with each other to build an
interface: even if they share a common look, the way they are laid out on a page is
specific to each project. Like TEI, TEI-Publisher is a modular
and flexible tool that allows editors and designers to represent a DSE in different
ways. It provides a framework to help them make their own rhetorical argument
(Andrews and van Zundert 2018, 8) about their data and their conception of a DL and
DSEs.

column6: Finally, our experience with TEI-Publisher leads us to consider

column7: that it does not only influence the design of our website, but also our data model.
Usually, a clear distinction is made between content and its form : when we work with XML, we start by examining the meaning of
the data, then think about their visualisation with scripts and stylesheets. However,
in this case, some of our editing choices have been determined by the way the tool
functions. For instance, the way we display facsimiles does not follow the
prescriptions made by the XML-TEI community but simplifies them.

column6: No project operates in isolation. It is influenced by the design of other projects, by

column7: the expectations of their scientific communities, by the type of digital edition
chosen or by the tools used, whether software (eXist-DB, TEI-Publisher, EVT) or libraries (Bootstrap). In the last case, the choice of standard technologies
argues for the awareness of a project about interoperability and sustainability
issues, and about what is advised and acknowledged by its scientific community.

column6: Conclusions
The design of our interface relies on ergonomic and scholarly considerations, that

column7: reflects the nature of our corpus and our goals. If we return to the three levels of
arguments defined by Andrews and van Zundert, from a usability perspective, the
interface of Untangling the cordel argues for a minimalist
design, that leaves space for data and personalisation. Whether it is with the list of
chapbooks or their notice, it does not impose a predefined way to interact with data,
but let users decide which functionalities or information they want to display.

column6: The conceptual level of our interface is related both to the model of a DL and of a

column7: DSE. On one hand, the interface argues that our DL follows the model of a physical
library. It reuses concepts and practices common to analogue libraries, such as the
way users select their books, and can thus be perceived as their extension. On the
other hand, it argues that our DSEs are reading editions, favourable to a solitary
concentration, by according a central place to text and facsimiles.

column6: Finally, regarding the third level and what the DL and DSEs say about our data, the

column7: layout of the interface underlines the intertextuality or intermediality of Spanish
chapbooks. By offering various levels of analysis, it allows to study components of a
chapbook separately (document, text, or woodcuts) or in relation with each other.

column6: In conclusion, working with the levels of arguments proposed by Andrews and van Zundert

column7: helped us in the creation of our interface by providing us a frame and a better
perception of the meaning we put in each component and design choices. We believe that
following this method is a way to encourage the study of interfaces and their
long-term preservation, thus joining the recommendations made by Claire Warwick in her
recent paper.

column6: No interface is neutral: deliberately or not, it tells something about a project at a

column7: given moment, its values, or its perceptions of a specific subject. When it comes to
the development of a digital interface, it is important to keep in mind that designing
is not just about the way an interface looks like (the dessin
in French), but also about its intention and meaning (the dessein).
